results.title: Shift of the lamplighter base group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $p$, the shift is the automorphism $f \mapsto f(\cdot - 1)$ of the base group $\bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Z}/p$, the additive group of finitely supported functions $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/p$, viewed as a multiplicative group.

results.title: Lamplighter group
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a natural number $p$, the lamplighter group $\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}$ is the semidirect product $\left(\bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{Z}/p\right) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}$, in which $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ acts on the base group by the $n$-th power of the shift $f \mapsto f(\cdot - 1)$.

results.title: Non-zero-divisor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An element $s$ of a ring $R$ is a non-zero-divisor when it is neither a left nor a right zero divisor: for every $z \in R$, $zs = 0$ implies $z = 0$ and $sz = 0$ implies $z = 0$.

results.title: Right Ore ring
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A ring $R$ satisfies the right Ore condition for its non-zero-divisors, so that it has a classical right ring of quotients, when for all $s, t \in R$ with $s$ a non-zero-divisor there are $x, y \in R$ with $x$ a non-zero-divisor and $sy = tx$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 12.47: some lamplighter group algebra is Ore
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: There are a field $k$ and a prime $p$ such that the group algebra $k[\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}]$ of the lamplighter group $\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies the right Ore condition for its non-zero-divisors, that is, has a classical right ring of quotients.

results.title: Lamplighter group algebras are not Ore
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every field $k$ and every prime $p$, the group algebra $k[\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}]$ of the lamplighter group $\mathbb{Z}/p \wr \mathbb{Z}$ does not satisfy the right Ore condition for its non-zero-divisors: there are $s$ and $t$ in it, with $s$ a non-zero-divisor, such that $sy = tx$ holds for no $x$ and $y$ with $x$ a non-zero-divisor.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Ergodicity is exactly primitivity of the transition matrix. This is the bridge to Mathlib: `Matrix.IsPrimitive` is the same condition for a bare matrix, while `IsErgodic` is the stochastic-matrix form, with nonnegativity supplied by the `StochasticMatrix` structure.

results.title: Powers of a stochastic matrix are stochastic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every row of every power of a stochastic matrix sums to `1`: powers of a stochastic matrix are stochastic.

results.title: First recursive power of a stochastic matrix
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: One step of the power recursion: `matPow 1` is the matrix itself.

results.title: Additivity of recursive matrix powers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Powers add: `matPow (a + b)` is the matrix product of `matPow a` and `matPow b`.

results.title: Later powers of a positive stochastic matrix power stay positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If some power `w` of a stochastic matrix is all-positive, then every later power `m ≥ w` is all-positive: write `m = (m - w) + w`, use `matPow_add`, and note that row `i` of `matPow (m - w)` sums to `1`, so some entry of that row is positive, and that entry times the positive `matPow w` entry gives a positive summand.

results.title: Pairwise positive powers of an ergodic chain
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An ergodic chain has, for every pair of states, some positive power with a positive `(i, j)`-entry. (This is the per-pair form; it is strictly weaker than ergodicity, which asks for one power working for all pairs at once.)

results.title: Powers of an ergodic chain are eventually all positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Once a power of an ergodic chain is all-positive, every later power is all-positive: there is a threshold `w` past which every power is all-positive.

results.title: Underlying matrix of a stochastic matrix power

results.title: Recursive powers of a stochastic matrix power
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Powers of a power: `(P.pow p).matPow n = P.matPow (p * n)`.

results.title: Powers of an ergodic Markov chain are ergodic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every positive power of an ergodic chain is ergodic.

results.title: Uniform Markov chain on finitely many states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The uniform chain: every transition has probability `1 / (M + 1)`.

results.title: Transition probabilities of the uniform chain
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The uniform chain has constant transition probabilities `1 / (M + 1)`.

results.title: The uniform Markov chain is ergodic
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Identity Markov chain
results.caption: Definition

results.caption: Theorem

results.caption: Theorem

results.title: The identity Markov chain is not ergodic
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Doeblin's argument
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Doeblin's argument (Levin, Peres and Wilmer, proof of Theorem 4.9): if the `r`-step transition probabilities dominate `δ π`, then the total variation distance of `Pⁿ(x, ·)` from the stationary distribution `π` is at most `(1 - δ) ^ ⌊n / r⌋`. The bound is informative when `r > 0` and `0 < δ`; for `r = 0` (`n / 0 = 0`) or `δ ≤ 0` it reads `d_TV ≤ 1` or weaker.

results.title: The convergence theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The convergence theorem (Levin, Peres and Wilmer, Theorem 4.9): a primitive (irreducible and aperiodic) stochastic matrix with stationary distribution `π` converges to `π` geometrically fast in total variation, uniformly in the starting state.

results.title: Convergence of matrix powers to the stationary distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a primitive stochastic matrix with stationary distribution `π`, every row of `Pⁿ` converges to `π`: `Pⁿ(x, y) → π(y)`.

results.title: Uniqueness of the stationary distribution of a primitive chain
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A primitive stochastic matrix has at most one stationary distribution. In fact `π'` may be any stationary vector of total mass `1`, not necessarily nonnegative.

results.title: Stationary distribution of a primitive chain has full support
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The stationary distribution of a primitive stochastic matrix has full support.

results.title: Unit triangles of the triangular lattice
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: Let $e_1 = (1, 0)$ and $e_2 = (1/2, \sqrt{3}/2)$, and write $p(i, j) = i e_1 + j e_2$ for integers $i, j$. results.title: Cycles in a graph
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A cycle in a simple graph $G$ consists of a base vertex $v$ of $G$ together with a closed walk $v = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_n = v$ in $G$ such that $n \ge 1$, the $n$ edges $v_{k-1} v_k$ of the walk are pairwise distinct, and the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$ are pairwise distinct. In a simple graph this forces $n \ge 3$.

results.title: Edges of a cycle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The edges of a cycle $c$ in a simple graph form the list of the edges of its closed walk, in the order in which $c$ traverses them starting from its base vertex; each edge is the unordered pair of its two endpoints.

results.title: Length of a cycle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The length of a cycle in a simple graph is the number of edges of its closed walk.

results.title: Cycle covers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph. A finite multiset $C$ of cycles in $G$ is a cycle cover of $G$ when every edge of $G$ is an edge of at least one cycle in $C$.

results.title: Total length of a multiset of cycles
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The total length of a finite multiset $C$ of cycles in a simple graph is the sum of the lengths of the cycles in $C$, each counted with its multiplicity.
